Concise Clinical Note

Consult Summary:
31-year-old man with 4-day history of intensely pruritic, erythematous, dry/cracked rash on chest, hands, and inner elbows; clinical impression most consistent with an atopic dermatitis (eczema) flare.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Sudden onset (4 days) of red, sore, very itchy rash on chest, hands, inner elbows; itch disrupts sleep and concentration.  
• Associated symptoms: No fever, systemic symptoms, cough, dyspnea, urinary or bowel changes. No bleeding, pus, or exudate; some skin cracking.  
• Pertinent negatives: No facial, leg, or scalp involvement; no new drugs; no known allergen exposure identified.  
• Past medical history: Previous eczema (arm-limited), childhood asthma (resolved).  
• Allergies: Denies drug or other allergies.  
• Medications: No regular meds. Tried OTC topical steroid cream (name unknown) and OTC oral antihistamines without relief.  
• Social / preventive: 31 y male; lives with flat-mates; project manager at pharmaceutical company; non-smoker; drinks a few beers weekly; enjoys hiking.

Examination:
(Video review—limited detail)  
• Skin: Erythematous, dry, cracked plaques/patches on chest, hands, inner elbows; no vesicles, weeping, or infection signs noted.  
• No vitals recorded; no other physical findings documented.

Impression:
Likely diagnoses (ranked):  
1. Atopic dermatitis flare – high probability given personal history, flexural involvement, dry/cracked skin, intense pruritus.  
2. Allergic/irritant contact dermatitis – possible acute trigger; consider if poor response to treatment or clear exposure identified.  
3. Scabies – lower probability; consider if persistent or household contacts become symptomatic.

Plan:
• Pharmacologic
  – Prescribe medium-/high-potency topical corticosteroid (stronger than OTC preparation) for affected areas.  
  – Prescribe emollient/bath/shower moisturizer; advise liberal, frequent use.  
  – Prescribe non-sedating antihistamine (Fexofenadine) for pruritus; may try alternative agents if inadequate.  
• Non-pharmacologic
  – Keep diary of potential triggers (soaps, detergents, fabrics, activities); avoid identified irritants/allergens.  
  – Lukewarm showers; pat dry, moisturize immediately.  
• Follow-up
  – Re-evaluate in 7–10 days; sooner if worsening, spreading, or signs of infection.  
  – Consider dermatology referral or alternative diagnoses (e.g., contact dermatitis patch testing, scabies evaluation) if no improvement.

Quality checks:

● Missing but expected: Objective vitals; detailed skin description (morphology, extent); name/strength of previous OTC steroid; formal allergy list.  
● Conflicts: Doctor briefly mentioned “back” involvement once—patient did not; transcript otherwise consistent.  
● Transcript quality: Audio issues, some repetitions; core clinical content adequate but physical-exam detail limited.
